claims.text: Local electronic heterogeneity is the key factor enabling the HEA catalyst's 12-electron ethanol oxidation behavior.
A range of distinct active sites facilitates rapid sequential electron and proton transfers.
The catalyst consists of a near-equiatomic mixture of platinum-group metals and complementary transition metals.
The catalyst is initially a random solid solution.
Inducing phase separation or narrowing the compositional spread will decrease local electronic heterogeneity.
The relevant ethanol oxidation regime normally follows a 12-electron pathway.
Surface heterogeneity manifests as variations in electron density and neighboring-site d-band centers.
Diverse active sites provide optimal adsorption energies for ethanol and its intermediates.
Electronic diversity promotes efficient electron transfer through multiple oxidation steps.
Electronic diversity suppresses poisoning by ethanol-oxidation intermediates.
Reducing electronic heterogeneity homogenizes the active sites.
Homogenizing the active sites slows the overall multi-electron ethanol oxidation process.
Greater local electronic heterogeneity will produce higher ethanol-oxidation current density.
Greater local electronic heterogeneity will increase selectivity toward complete ethanol oxidation products.
Greater local electronic heterogeneity will enhance catalyst durability.
A standard random, near-equiatomic HEA has demonstrated strong ethanol oxidation performance.
The proposed electronic-heterogeneity effect should be strongest under the established ethanol electrochemical conditions.
At extreme pH or temperature, or in another reaction regime, factors other than electronic heterogeneity may dominate.

contradictions.description: The intervention is described as modifying or narrowing composition while keeping the overall elemental makeup constant, and the experiment likewise proposes adjusting composition while maintaining the same elemental ratios. A phase-state change at fixed composition is possible, but a bulk compositional narrowing is not clearly compatible with unchanged overall ratios.

The design requires a reduced-heterogeneity catalyst, but the rule treats similar electronic-structure profiles as falsification. Similar profiles would instead show that the intended mediator manipulation was not achieved, so they cannot by themselves falsify the mechanism.
